[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Memory Management and Garbage Collection in Ruby on Rails"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding how Ruby manages memory and executes garbage collection (GC) is crucial for scaling Ruby on Rails applications. While Rails abstracts much of the low-level complexity, web applications often face memory bloat due to heavy request cycles, database querying, and caching."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"How Ruby's Garbage Collector Works"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ruby uses a generational, incremental mark-and-sweep garbage collector (introduced and heavily optimized in Ruby 2.1 and later). The core concept relies on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. Therefore, Ruby splits objects into generations to optimize cleanup."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Young Generation: Newly allocated objects live here. They are collected frequently via minor GC sweeps."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Old Generation: Objects that survive multiple minor GC cycles are promoted to the old generation, which is swept less frequently via major GC."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Common Memory Bottlenecks in Rails"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"In a Rails monolith, memory bloat often manifests as copy-on-write (COW) copy degradation. When a worker process (like Puma) handles requests, it loads the Rails environment into memory. If processes modify shared memory extensively, COW fails, causing RAM usage to skyrocket."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Loading massive Active Record result sets into arrays without pagination or streaming."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Memory leaks in long-running background workers (e.g., Sidekiq) caused by gem dependencies or unreleased cache."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"String manipulation and large JSON serialization in API responses."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Tuning GC Parameters via Environment Variables"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ruby allows you to fine-tune garbage collection using environment variables. Adjusting these values can drastically improve throughput and reduce memory fragmentation in production."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"export RUBY_GC_HEAP_INIT_SLOTS=600000
export RUBY_GC_HEAP_GROWTH_FACTOR=1.25
export RUBY_GC_HEAP_GROWTH_MAX_SLOTS=400000
export RUBY_GC_OLD_OBJECT_LIMIT_FACTOR=0.9"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Profiling Memory Usage"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"To diagnose memory bloat, developers rely on gems like 'memory_profiler' and 'benchmark-ips'. You can inspect object allocations in specific blocks of code to find memory hogs."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"report = MemoryProfiler.report do
  # Code block to profile
  User.includes(:posts).all.to_a
end

report.pretty_print"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Rails Memory Optimization"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use find_each or find_in_batches instead of .all to process large database tables in chunks."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Configure Puma worker-killer or actively monitor RSS (Resident Set Size) memory limits in production environments."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Upgrade to the latest stable Ruby version to leverage upstream GC performance improvements."}]
